source.title: Make and Keep Friends
source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on research from the University of Kansas, Berkeley's Greater Good Science Center, Kaiser Permanente and Utah State University Extension.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: University of Kansas, Study reveals number of hours it takes to make a friend, https://news.ku.edu/news/article/2018/03/06/study-reveals-number-hours-it-takes-make-friend; Greater Good Science Center, How long does it take to make a friend?, https://greatergood.berkeley.edu/article/item/how_long_does_it_take_to_make_a_friend; Kaiser Permanente, How to make new friends as an adult, https://healthy.kaiserpermanente.org/health-wellness/healtharticle.social-connection-benefits; Utah State University Extension, The benefits of adult friendships, https://extension.usu.edu/relationships/faq/the-benefits-of-adult-friendships

cards.title: Friendship is good for your health and happiness
cards.body:
Friends are not a luxury. Good friendships give you a sense of belonging, make good times better and help you cope with stress and hard times.

Research links strong social connections with lower risk of depression, high blood pressure and other health problems, and with longer life in older age. Loneliness, on the other hand, can be as harmful as some well-known health risks.

Yet making friends often gets harder as we grow up. Work, family duties and moving to new places push friendships down the list. The good news is that friendship is a skill, not luck. The parts of this guide show simple, practical ways to find friends and keep them.
cards.apply_it: Write down the names of three people who make your life better. Send one of them a short message today.

quiz.question: What does research suggest about strong friendships?
options: They make little difference to health
They only matter for children
They are linked to better mental and physical health
They cause more stress than they relieve
quiz.explanation: Strong social connection is linked to lower risk of depression and other health problems, and to longer life.

cards.title: Go where people gather regularly
cards.body:
Friends rarely appear while you sit at home. You need to be around people, ideally the same people more than once.

Good places include clubs, sports teams, gyms, faith communities, classes, choirs, hobby groups, study groups and volunteering. Volunteering is especially good because you meet people who share your values while doing something worthwhile. Online groups can work too, especially if they lead to meeting in person.

Choose activities you genuinely enjoy, so you keep going even before the friendships form. Say yes to invitations more often than feels natural, and chat to neighbours or regulars at a local shop or café. Every friendly conversation is a small step.
cards.apply_it: Find one group, class or volunteering activity near you that meets regularly, and sign up or go along once this month.

quiz.question: Why is volunteering a good way to meet friends?
options: You meet people with shared values while doing something worthwhile
You are paid to make friends
It means you never need to talk
It guarantees a best friend
quiz.explanation: Volunteering brings you into regular contact with people who care about the same things you do.

cards.title: Friendship grows from repeated time together
cards.body:
A University of Kansas study by Jeffrey Hall found that it takes roughly fifty hours together to go from acquaintance to casual friend, around ninety hours to become friends and more than two hundred hours to become close friends.

That sounds like a lot, but it shows why repeated contact matters. Seeing the same people week after week, at a class or club, slowly builds familiarity and trust. One great conversation is a start, not a friendship.

The type of time counts too. Relaxed time, like sharing a meal, joking around or playing a game, builds closeness more than time spent only working side by side. So when you get on with a colleague or classmate, suggest doing something together outside of work.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you get on with at work, school or a club. Invite them for a coffee, a walk or lunch this week.

quiz.question: According to the Kansas research, roughly how many hours does it take to become close friends?
options: About 5 hours
About 20 hours
About 50 hours
More than 200 hours
quiz.explanation: The study estimated about 50 hours for a casual friend, about 90 for a friend and over 200 for a close friend.

cards.title: Be curious about other people
cards.body:
People warm to those who show real interest in them. Instead of worrying about seeming impressive, focus on being interested.

Ask open questions that invite a story: "How did you get into that?" "What's the best part of your week been?" Then follow up on what they say. Remember details, like the name of their sister or the exam they were nervous about, and ask about them next time.

This also takes pressure off you. You don't need clever lines; you just need curiosity. Look for shared interests and experiences, but enjoy differences too. Over time, move beyond small talk to talking about real life, hopes and opinions, which builds closeness much faster.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, ask one open question and one follow-up question before you talk about yourself.

quiz.question: Which question is more likely to start a real conversation?
options: Nice weather, isn't it?
How did you get into that?
Are you busy?
Do you like it here?
quiz.explanation: Open questions invite people to share stories, which builds connection.

cards.title: Listen so people feel truly heard
cards.body:
Being a good listener is one of the most valued qualities in a friend. Most people rarely feel fully listened to, so when you do it well, they notice.

Put your phone away, look at the person and give them your full attention. Nod and respond so they know you are following. Ask questions to understand, and sum up what you heard: "So it sounds like you felt left out."

Resist the urge to jump in with your own story or fix the problem straight away. Often people want to be understood more than advised. If you're not sure, ask: "Do you want advice, or do you just need to talk?" That one question can save a lot of misunderstanding.
cards.apply_it: Next time a friend shares a problem, ask "Do you want advice, or do you just need to talk?" and follow their answer.

quiz.question: What is a good habit when a friend shares a problem?
options: Immediately tell them what to do
Change the subject to your own problems
Ask whether they want advice or just want to talk
Check your phone while they speak
quiz.explanation: Asking what they need avoids giving unwanted advice and helps them feel heard.

cards.title: Small acts of kindness build big bonds
cards.body:
Friendships are built less from grand gestures than from many small acts of care. A message on someone's birthday, a lift to the station, bringing food when they are ill or remembering an important day all add up.

Say thank you often, even for small things, and tell people what you appreciate about them. Celebrate their good news warmly. People remember who was genuinely happy for them.

Kindness should be freely given, not keeping score. If you notice you always give and never receive, that's worth a conversation, but most healthy friendships balance out over time. Small kindnesses make people feel valued, and people return to those who make them feel that way.
cards.apply_it: Do one small, unexpected kind thing for a friend today, such as sending a note saying what you appreciate about them.

quiz.question: What builds strong friendships most often?
options: Expensive gifts
Keeping careful score of favours
Only helping in emergencies
Many small acts of care and thanks over time
quiz.explanation: Regular small kindnesses show people they matter, which deepens the bond.

cards.title: Be the one who reaches out first
cards.body:
Many people wait to be invited, worried that others are too busy or not interested. Research suggests we often underestimate how much people like us and how much they welcome hearing from us.

So take the first step. Suggest a specific plan, such as "Do you want to get lunch on Saturday?", rather than a vague "We should hang out sometime." Specific invitations are much easier to say yes to.

If someone says no, don't take it personally. People really are busy. Try once more another time. If they keep declining without suggesting another date, it is fine to put your energy into other people. Friendship needs both people to want it.
cards.apply_it: Send one specific invitation today, with a day and an activity, to someone you would like to know better.

quiz.question: Which invitation is more likely to lead to meeting up?
options: Do you want to get lunch on Saturday?
We should hang out sometime
Let me know if you're ever free
Maybe one day we could do something
quiz.explanation: Specific plans are much easier to agree to than vague ideas.

cards.title: Be reliable: show up and keep confidences
cards.body:
Trust is the backbone of friendship, and it is built through reliability. Do what you say you will do. Turn up when you say you will, and if you can't, tell people early and suggest another time.

Keep confidences. When someone shares something private, it stays with you. Gossiping about one friend to another quickly teaches everyone that you can't be trusted.

Be there in hard times as well as good ones. Visiting someone who is ill, attending a funeral or just sitting with someone who is sad often matters more than any party. People remember who showed up when life was difficult, and those are the friendships that last.
cards.apply_it: Think of one promise you have made to a friend recently. Keep it this week, or let them know honestly if plans have changed.

quiz.question: What is one of the quickest ways to damage trust in friendship?
options: Asking questions
Sharing a friend's secrets with others
Saying no to an invitation once
Being busy at work
quiz.explanation: Gossiping about private things shows people their confidences aren't safe with you.

cards.title: Open up a little at a time
cards.body:
Closeness grows when people share more of themselves. If you only ever talk about surface things, a friendship can stay polite but shallow for years.

You don't need to share everything at once. Start small: an honest opinion, something you are looking forward to, or something that worried you this week. When the other person opens up in return, you can go a little deeper. This gradual back-and-forth builds trust on both sides.

Use "I" statements to share feelings: "I felt nervous about moving here" rather than "This place is unfriendly." Being a bit vulnerable gives others permission to be real too, and that is where true friendship starts.
cards.apply_it: Share one honest, slightly personal thing with a friend this week, such as a worry or a hope, and see how they respond.

quiz.question: How does closeness usually grow between friends?
options: Sharing everything on the first meeting
Never talking about feelings
Only talking about the news and sport
Gradually sharing more of yourself on both sides
quiz.explanation: Step-by-step openness from both people builds trust and depth.

cards.title: Stay in touch, especially when life gets busy
cards.body:
Friendships rarely end with a fight. Much more often they fade because nobody gets in touch. Busy jobs, children, moving away and caring for family all make it easy to drift.

Make staying in touch a habit. Set up regular plans, like a monthly call, a weekly game or an annual trip. Between meet-ups, send a quick message, a photo or a voice note that says "this made me think of you."

For friends far away, video calls and messages keep the thread alive until you can meet. You don't need hours. A few minutes of contact, done regularly, is often enough to keep a friendship warm through busy seasons of life.
cards.apply_it: Choose one friend you have drifted from and send them a short message today saying you thought of them.

quiz.question: How do most friendships end, according to this guide?
options: With a big argument
With a formal goodbye
By slowly fading when nobody gets in touch
Because of moving house
quiz.explanation: Most friendships fade through lack of contact, which regular small messages can prevent.

cards.title: Repair a rift instead of letting it harden
cards.body:
Even good friends hurt each other sometimes. A forgotten birthday, a careless comment or a misunderstanding can create distance. Left alone, small hurts can harden into silence.

If you caused the hurt, apologise sincerely and simply: say what you did, that you are sorry and how you will do better, without making excuses. If you were hurt, raise it calmly and early, using "I" statements: "I felt hurt when I wasn't invited." Then listen to their side. There may be a reason you didn't know.

Most friendships survive honest conversations, and many grow stronger. What damages them is avoiding the problem and quietly building resentment.
cards.apply_it: If there is a small tension with a friend, send a calm, honest message this week to clear the air or apologise.

quiz.question: What makes a good apology to a friend?
options: Saying what you did, that you are sorry and how you will do better
Explaining why it wasn't really your fault
Waiting for them to forget about it
Apologising only if they apologise first
quiz.explanation: A sincere apology names the action, takes responsibility and commits to change, without excuses.

cards.title: Let go of friendships that harm you
cards.body:
Not every friendship is good for you. Some people repeatedly put you down, use you, pressure you into things you don't want to do, or only get in touch when they need something.

Ask yourself how you usually feel after seeing them. Drained, anxious or smaller? Or supported and like yourself? If it is mostly the first, try setting clear boundaries or talking honestly. If nothing changes, it is okay to spend less time with them or end the friendship.

You don't owe anyone a dramatic exit; you can simply step back. Letting go makes room for people who treat you well. If a friendship involves threats, abuse or danger, talk to someone you trust or a support service for help.
cards.apply_it: Think about how you feel after time with each of your close friends. Notice who leaves you feeling better, and plan to see them soon.

quiz.question: What is a useful sign a friendship may be harming you?
options: You disagree sometimes
You usually feel drained, anxious or smaller after seeing them
They are busy some weeks
They have other friends
quiz.explanation: How you regularly feel after time together is a good guide to whether a friendship is healthy.
